items.summary: The organization of distributed neural activity remains one of the central challenges in computational neuroscience. Contemporary frameworks, including Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, entropy-based approaches, and electromagnetic field theories, have advanced our understanding of neural coordination but employ different mathematical descriptions of large-scale brain dynamics. Within this frame, we assert that fast rhythms created corticothalamically with the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) can become time-locked with regions throughout the brain via nascent oscillations as well as sensory organs and viscera. items.summary: Aim: Childhood stress can alter adolescent stress responses, predisposing individuals to neurochemical imbalances associated with psychosis later in life. Antipsychotic treatments are limited by extrapyramidal and metabolic side effects with insignificant impact on stress-related abnormalities in schizophrenia. Flavonoids such as apigenin may offer a safer therapeutic alternative with broader neuroprotective effects. This window coincides with maturation of brain structures critical to reward and decision-making, including the prefrontal cortex, as well as peripheral physiological systems such as the gut microbiome - making it a period of heightened vulnerability to the long-lasting effects of drug exposure. items.summary: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains an aggressive adult primary brain tumor despite surgery, radiotherapy and temozolomide-based chemotherapy, partly because glioblastoma stem cells (GSCs) retain self-renewal capacity, lineage plasticity and therapeutic resistance. Cancer neuroscience has shown that glioma cells receive activity-dependent neuronal signals and exploit neural circuits to support tumor growth and invasion. items.summary: Abstract Youth irritability, characterized as proneness to anger/frustration, is associated with negative mental health outcomes. This study identified irritability trajectories across the transition to early adolescence and applied machine learning to identify preadolescent predictors of irritability trajectories. Data are from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a large longitudinal study that tracks youth development from preadolescence ( n = 11,862, ages 8.92–11.08 years, M = 9.91, SD = 0.62). Current studies of IME tissue responses provide whole-transcriptome multicellular spots, targeted transcript coordinates, regional ribonucleic acid (RNA) or protein profiles, registered morphology, and exploratory associations between tissue measurements and recording performance. Implant-centered distance locates these measurements relative to the device. items.summary: Abstract Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) has emerged as a powerful optical imaging technique for studying complex biological systems, particularly in neuroscience. By selectively illuminating a thin optical plane and combining it with camera-based widefield detection, LSFM enables rapid volumetric imaging with reduced photobleaching and phototoxicity compared to point-scanning approaches, such as confocal and multiphoton microscopy. items.summary: Variations in neural circuitry, inherited or acquired, may underlie important individual differences in thought, feeling, and action patterns. Here, we used task-free connectivity analyses to isolate and characterize two distinct networks typically coactivated during functional MRI tasks. We identified a "salience network," anchored by dorsal anterior cingulate (dACC) and orbital frontoinsular cortices with robust connectivity to subcortical and limbic structures, and an "executive-control network" that links dorsolateral frontal and parietal neocortices. These intrinsic connectivity networks

items.title: Targeting the Gut to Modify Parkinson's Disease: From Mechanisms to Potential Therapeutics
items.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder and its prevalence continues to rise with population aging. Its cardinal motor features arise from the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, accompanied by intraneuronal α-synuclein aggregates known as Lewy bodies. Neuropathological evidence suggests that, in a subset of patients, α-synuclein pathology first appears in the enteric nervous system and ascends to the brain via the gut-brain axis. items.title: Beyond retest gains: episodic memory practice effects and longitudinal cognitive trajectories in cognitively healthy adults
items.summary: Background Practice effects in repeated neuropsychological assessment are usually treated as measurement bias, although they may carry meaningful information. It remains unclear whether individual differences in episodic memory practice effects are associated with cognitive level and longitudinal change beyond generic retest-related gains. Methods We analyzed data from 442 cognitively healthy middle-aged and older adults who completed neuropsychological assessments in 2018, 2021, and 2025. items.title: Mapping the neural basis of the perception of “flow of time”: interval timing and mental time travel in the human brain
items.summary: Although neurodegenerative diseases and brain injuries have been reported to impair the perception of “the flow of time,” the underlying neural mechanisms remain uncertain. We examined symptoms related to interval timing and mental time travel, two neuropsychological phenomena associated with the perception of the flow of time that have been relatively well characterized. In addition, we reviewed the current evidence and proposed a potential underlying brain mechanism.

items.summary: Workplace violence (WPV) remains a critical public health concern among Taiwanese public servants despite regulatory frameworks such as the Occupational Safety and Health Act. This national cross-sectional study (N = 20,046) examined the prevalence of WPV and its associations with mental health and sleep duration among Taiwanese public servants. Using probabilistic sampling, participants were recruited from four major employment sectors: civil service, public enterprises, medical services, and public schools. items.summary: BACKGROUND: As mortality rates decline, life expectancy increases, and populations age, non-fatal outcomes of diseases and injuries are becoming a larger component of the global burden of disease. The Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2016 (GBD 2016) provides a comprehensive assessment of prevalence, incidence, and years lived with disability (YLDs) for 328 causes in 195 countries and territories from 1990 to 2016. METHODS: We estimated prevalence and incidence for 328 diseases and injuries and 2982 sequelae, their non-fatal consequences. We used DisMod-MR 2.1, a Baye

items.title: FieldTrip: Open Source Software for Advanced Analysis of MEG, EEG, and Invasive Electrophysiological Data
items.summary: This paper describes FieldTrip, an open source software package that we developed for the analysis of MEG, EEG, and other electrophysiological data. The software is implemented as a MATLAB toolbox and includes a complete set of consistent and user-friendly high-level functions that allow experimental neuroscientists to analyze experimental data. It includes algorithms for simple and advanced analysis, such as time-frequency analysis using multitapers, source reconstruction using dipoles, distributed sources and beamformers, connectivity analysis, and nonparametric statistical permutation tests

items.title: Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review
items.summary: BACKGROUND: The quality and quantity of individuals' social relationships has been linked not only to mental health but also to both morbidity and mortality. OBJECTIVES: This meta-analytic review was conducted to determine the extent to which social relationships influence risk for mortality, which aspects of social relationships are most highly predictive, and which factors may moderate the risk. Image processing with ImageJ
items.summary: Wayne Rasband of NIH has created ImageJ, an open source Java-written program that is now at version 1.31 and is used for many imaging applications, including those that that span the gamut from skin analysis to neuroscience. ImageJ is in the public domain and runs on any operating system (OS). ImageJ is easy to use and can do many imaging manipulations. A very large and knowledgeable group makes up the user community for ImageJ. Topics covered are imaging abilities; cross platform; image formats support as of June 2004; extensions, including macros and plug-ins; and imaging library. NIH report

items.summary: Abstract Non-invasive recordings using brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies. This makes it challenging to establish

items.title: Self-regulated emergence of heavy-tailed weight distributions in evolving complex network architectures
items.summary: The nervous system continuously adjusts connection strengths and reorganizes its structure to form and maintain complex connectivity patterns with heavy-tailed weight distributions. We propose a parsimonious model in which structural and synaptic plasticity are driven by common diffusion dynamics. Synaptic plasticity alone generates heavy-tailed weight distributions, but only when activity spreading remains predominantly local. However, when combined with structural plasticity through adaptive rewiring, the model also generates these distributions with more extensive activity flow. Furthermore

items.title: Impulsivity, cognitive inflexibility, and brain network dysregulation in etomidate use disorder: A clinical and EEG microstate study
items.summary: Etomidate, a short-acting GABA_A receptor modulator and emerging novel psychoactive substance, is increasingly abused non-medically. Despite rising clinical concern, the neuropsychological profiles of etomidate use disorder (EUD) remain poorly characterized, prompting this systematic investigation of its clinical and neurophysiological features. 152 individuals with EUD and 67 age-matched healthy controls (HC) were recruited. Participants completed a series of standardized assessments measuring craving, impulsivity, inhibitory control, and habitual behavior. Resting-state EEG data were analyze

items.summary: Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) is an ageing and progressive neurodegenerative disease, and one of the most prevalent dementias that affects millions of patients worldwide, including millions of people in Europe, and is a public health priority. Early and right diagnosis is of paramount importance for early therapeutic intervention as well as retardation of the disease. The visual search for small changes in the brain is rather time-consuming and subjective. items.title: Case Report: Isolated leptomeningeal relapse after systemic control in PALB2-altered pancreatic cancer
items.summary: Background Leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) is an uncommon manifestation of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and has a median survival of only 1–2 months after diagnosis. Isolated LM after prolonged extracranial disease control is particularly rare and may be overlooked when systemic imaging results look stable. Case presentation We describe a 51-year-old man with metastatic PDAC who initially received a treatment regimen comprising KN046 and gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel, followed by a prolonged course of folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, and oxaliplatin (FOLFIRINOX), and subseque

items.title: Candidate neurobiological pathways linking physical exercise to cognition in Parkinson’s disease: a hypothesis-generating translational framework
items.summary: Cognitive impairment is a major nonmotor symptom of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet effective strategies for preserving cognitive function remain limited. Although physical exercise may confer cognitive benefits, the biological pathways linking exercise to cognition in PD remain incompletely established. This narrative review presents a hypothesis-generating translational framework for 4 candidate mechanistic domains that may contribute to exercise-related cognitive effects in PD. First, exercise-responsive neurotrophic signaling, particularly through brain-derived neurotrophic factor-tropomyosi

items.summary: Background The optimal management of critical primary brainstem hemorrhage (PBSH, hematoma volume 5–15 mL) remains controversial. While minimally invasive surgery shows promise, multicenter evidence—particularly stratified by hematoma volume—is lacking. This study aimed to evaluate the survival benefit and safety of frameless robot-assisted aspiration compared to conservative treatment in patients with critical PBSH. items.summary: With the acceleration of urbanization, the importance of landscape architecture design in improving the quality of urban ecological environment and the quality of life of residents is becoming more and more prominent. To enhance the scientificity and practicability of the landscape design scheme, the study uses principal component analysis to downscale the multidimensional data of landscape architecture. It also combines Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA) to optimize the initial weights and biases of Back Propagation (BP) neural network, so as to realize the accurate evaluation and adjustment of t
items.source: Journal of Environmental Engineering and Landscape Management

items.title: Central Nervous System Vasculitis Mimicking Glioma in a Patient With Ulcerative Colitis: A Case Report and Literature Review
items.summary: A patient with ulcerative colitis presented with progressive memory impairment and alexia, with brain imaging showing a mass-like lesion mimicking glioma. Histopathology confirmed central nervous system (CNS) vasculitis. The patient's memory and reading ability improved and finally recovered following corticosteroid treatment, with no recurrence during the long-term follow-up. The case report and literature review highlight that clinicians should consider CNS vasculitis in patients with ulcerative colitis and tumor-like brain lesions.

sections.title: Research News
sections.description: Brain and neuroscience related research news from configured RSS feeds.

items.title: Scientists uncover a hidden map of the brain with 539 distinct regions
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered a hidden layer of organization in the brain by creating the first detailed 3D map of its lipids, the fatty molecules essential for brain structure and communication. By analyzing millions of measurements from mouse brains, researchers identified 539 distinct chemical zones, revealing patterns and boundaries that traditional brain maps have missed. Surprisingly, even white matter, once thought to be relatively uniform, contains a complex patchwork of chemically distinct regions.

items.title: After 30 years, scientists finally have a drug for a deadly brain disease
items.summary: The FDA has approved the first drug that directly targets Alexander disease, a devastating neurological disorder affecting fewer than one in a million people. Developed through decades of research, Zanvastro showed promising results in clinical trials, stabilizing motor function and even improving movement in some patients.

items.title: Scientists discover 5 hidden brain patterns behind depression
items.summary: Depression may not be one biological condition, but several distinct patterns of brain activity hiding under the same diagnosis. Researchers studying 263 people with depression identified five brain profiles, each showing different patterns of communication between brain regions and associations with symptoms such as anxiety, trauma, and substance abuse.

items.title: Drug target could block brain inflammation linked to Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s
items.summary: Blocking a receptor called P2X7 significantly reduced inflammation in human brain tissue, revealing a potential new treatment strategy for neurological and psychiatric disorders. The discovery could help researchers repurpose existing drugs for conditions including traumatic brain injury, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, depression, and schizophrenia.

items.title: What happens in the brain when cannabis makes you anxious?
items.summary: Cannabinoids may intensify anxiety by removing a natural brake on specific neurons in the brain’s fear center, particularly during stressful situations. In mice, shutting down those neurons sharply reduced cannabinoid-related anxious behavior.

items.title: Scientists create a needle-thin brain implant that can do three jobs at once
items.summary: A new needle-thin brain implant can record neural activity, deliver drugs, and stimulate multiple brain regions using a single flexible fiber. Successful tests in mice suggest it could give scientists a more precise, less invasive way to study the brain and may eventually help treat neurological disorders such as epilepsy.

items.title: Textbooks may have misdrawn this basic brain structure for 100 years
items.summary: Scientists discovered that brain-cell axons may not be smooth tubes as textbooks have shown for more than a century, but instead naturally resemble strings of tiny pearls. Those pearl-like structures can change with neural activity and may help control how quickly electrical signals travel through the brain.

items.title: Scientists recreated what mice saw from brain activity alone
items.summary: Scientists reconstructed videos from the brain activity of mice, producing 10-second clips based only on signals from neurons in the visual cortex. The breakthrough could help reveal how the brain reshapes what we see before it becomes our perception of reality.

items.title: Vagus Nerve Stimulation Could Help New Skills Stick
items.summary: Stimulating the vagus nerve after practice helped mice develop stronger long-term motor learning, revealing a potentially important window when the brain is still locking in a new skill. The effect was linked to rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, hinting that body-to-brain signals may help prepare the brain for lasting change.

items.title: Your gut bacteria may reveal how fast your brain is aging
items.summary: A UCLA study links faster brain aging to specific gut bacteria and chemical byproducts, with older-looking brains also associated with poorer memory, focus, and mood. The findings suggest that biological signs of brain aging may appear decades before obvious symptoms and could eventually make the gut a target for prevention.

items.title: Your gut may be making a molecule that raises Alzheimer’s risk
items.summary: Scientists have linked a gut bacterial compound called ImP to greater Alzheimer’s risk, harmful brain protein buildup, and faster cognitive decline. The finding raises the possibility that reducing ImP in the blood could one day help slow or prevent dementia.

items.title: This diet may slow brain aging by 2.5 years
items.summary: People who followed the MIND diet more closely showed slower brain shrinkage and less grey matter loss over time, with the strongest differences equivalent to about 2.5 years of delayed brain aging. Berries and poultry were linked with healthier brain changes, while sweets and fried fast foods were associated with greater tissue loss.

items.title: Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may have a reversible weakness
items.summary: The Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 may actively damage brain blood vessels and sabotage the cellular systems that remove harmful proteins. Researchers were able to reverse some of these effects in experiments, revealing promising new targets for Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, and other neurodegenerative diseases.

items.title: Brain scans reveal which disorders are linked to faster brain aging
items.summary: A massive MRI study found that Alzheimer’s disease, mild cognitive impairment, psychiatric disorders, and addiction are associated with distinct patterns of accelerated brain aging. The strongest effects appeared in Alzheimer’s and mild cognitive impairment, while ADHD and autism showed no significant overall difference.

items.title: Scientists just discovered what coffee really does to your gut and brain
items.summary: A new study suggests coffee may influence mood and brain function by changing the activity of microbes in the gut. Both caffeinated and decaf coffee were linked to lower stress, depression, and impulsivity, while also producing measurable changes in gut bacteria and metabolites. Decaf was associated with better learning and memory, while caffeinated coffee appeared to reduce anxiety and improve attention.

items.title: Resetting the body clock could help the brain recover after stroke
items.summary: Strengthening the body’s natural daily rhythms helped mice recover after stroke by improving the brain’s waste-clearing system and reducing lingering inflammation. The approach worked even when treatment began three days after the stroke, suggesting circadian-based therapies could eventually offer a new way to support long-term recovery.

items.title: Scientists found a surprising driver of Alzheimer’s outside the brain
items.summary: Scientists found that immune cells contributing to Alzheimer’s-related brain damage may be activated in lymph nodes outside the brain before traveling into the nervous system. Blocking this pathway in mice dramatically reduced neurodegeneration and preserved cognitive abilities, pointing to a potentially more accessible treatment target.

items.title: Glucosamine, a popular joint supplement, linked to faster Alzheimer’s progression
items.summary: A large health-record analysis found that glucosamine use was associated with a 25% higher likelihood of mild cognitive impairment progressing to dementia. Lab experiments suggest the popular joint supplement may intensify an abnormal sugar-tagging process in the Alzheimer’s brain, although researchers say clinical trials are needed to determine whether it actually causes harm.

items.title: REM sleep paradox: Dreaming may drain the brain’s energy even as fuel supply rises
items.summary: Scientists discovered a surprising energy paradox in the brain during REM sleep, the stage most closely associated with dreaming. Blood supply to the brain begins increasing even before REM starts, but neurons’ immediately available energy, measured as ATP, then drops. The finding suggests that dreaming may require such intense internal processing that neurons consume energy faster than it can be replenished.

items.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
items.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

items.title: Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep
items.summary: Caffeine may make sleep less restorative even when you fall asleep normally and stay in bed for eight hours, with EEG recordings revealing fewer of the slow brain waves associated with deep sleep. Individual sensitivity varies dramatically, meaning even caffeine consumed earlier in the day could affect nighttime recovery for some people.

items.title: Brain scans reveal a possible cause of long COVID fatigue and brain fog
items.summary: Researchers have found evidence that long COVID may damage dopamine releasing neurons in the brain, potentially explaining persistent fatigue, low motivation, slowed movement, and memory difficulties. The discovery could lead to new treatments that target the brain's dopamine system.

items.title: Stem cells reverse stroke damage and restore movement in mice
items.summary: Stem cell transplants helped regenerate stroke-damaged brain tissue in mice, producing new neurons and restoring lost motor function. The treatment also improved blood vessels, inflammation, and the blood-brain barrier, raising hopes that a similar approach could eventually help repair the human brain after stroke.

items.title: Stanford scientists discover the human brain may actually be two separate organs
items.summary: Scientists have found that the human brain develops from two distinct cellular systems, suggesting that evolution fused together two ancient nervous systems with very different jobs. The discovery also allowed researchers to grow human hindbrain neurons in the lab, opening new possibilities for studying ALS, spinal muscular atrophy, and other brainstem diseases.

items.title: Scientists restore a brain protein and reverse signs of aging in mice
items.summary: Scientists found that declining levels of the brain protein Menin may help drive aging, with lower levels in mice linked to inflammation, cognitive decline, weaker bones, and thinner skin. Restoring Menin reversed several age-related changes, while the amino acid D-serine improved cognition, hinting at a potentially intriguing new target for healthy aging.

items.title: Hidden “immune organ” in the skull may help fight brain cancer
items.summary: Scientists discovered a hidden “immune organ” inside the skull that acts as a rapid first responder against brain cancer in mice. Strengthening this local immune defense improved tumor rejection and survival, raising the possibility of new treatments that target the skull directly.

items.title: Scientists discover a major brain shift between ages 50 and 75
items.summary: Scientists have uncovered sweeping changes in how the human brain controls and organizes its genome beginning in midlife, offering new clues to why aging sharply increases the risk of Alzheimer’s and other neurodegenerative diseases. One of the biggest shifts occurred between about ages 50 and 75, when many of the brain’s original immune cells declined and were replaced by cells with more inflammatory characteristics. Researchers also found weakening of cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier, along with widespread deterioration in the genome’s three-dimensional organization.

items.title: Hidden brain wiring may help keep the mind sharp as gray matter shrinks
items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the brain’s short-range wiring may help protect cognition even as gray matter shrinks with age. Healthier connections just beneath the brain’s surface were linked to better language skills and appeared to weaken the impact of gray matter loss.

items.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
items.summary: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

items.title: Scientists reveal how the brain changes its connections when uncertainty strikes
items.summary: The brain has a remarkably flexible system for handling uncertainty and changing situations. Researchers found that the frontoparietal cortex constantly shifts how it communicates with other brain regions depending on what information is needed to make a decision. Rather than simply becoming more active when things get difficult, this network appears to reorganize itself in real time.

growingCitationPapers.title: Robust and replicable effects of ageing on resting-state brain electrophysiology measured with MEG
growingCitationPapers.summary: Abstract Non-invasive recordings using brain electrophysiology provide credible insights into decline in neuronal functioning with age. New approaches are required to translate these results into compelling clinical metrics and meet the global challenge of preserving brain health in ageing. Changes in neuronal dynamics with ageing are observable in the power spectra of EEG and MEG recordings. Highly promising candidates for electrophysiological markers have been identified, but progress is hindered by substantial methodological variability across studies.
